headline: A violent weekend in the Gulf (a Houthi strike killed 12 at Riyadh's airport, Iran says a tanker hit a mine in Hormuz, and Trump says the US may join the fight) puts oil risk back on top before bank earnings, CPI and TSMC.
summary: Markets are closed; all prices are Friday Oct 9 closes. The news since Friday is mostly geopolitical: Saudi authorities say a Saturday attack on King Khalid airport in Riyadh killed 12 and injured 309, Washington blames the Houthis, and Trump said the US may join Saudi strikes and will 'take a look' at his Oct 8 pledge not to strike Iran before the Nov 3 midterms. Iran's Revolutionary Guard also says a supertanker hit a mine on Saturday on a route it calls unauthorized; that claim is not independently confirmed. Brent settled at $104.72 on Friday, so Monday's open is the first test of how much of this is priced. Isaias is now a smaller story: Gulf offshore shut ins peaked near 72% on Friday, Chevron is sending crews back through Sunday, and there is still no damage report from the Pascagoula or Saraland refineries. The conflicting reports on China's rare earth deadline are settled as far as sources allow: the truce now runs to January 10, 2027, not November 10. No swing setup broke out on Friday, all on light volume, so nothing changes until prices move on real volume.

regime.why: Stocks closed the week near highs and VIX was calm at 14.84, but that was before the weekend attacks. With Brent above $104, the 10 year at 5.24% and a hot CPI able to revive hike talk, an oil spike on Monday would hit rate sensitive and travel names first. Keep normal size only on breakouts that confirm on volume, and expect a wider range in the first hour Monday.

signals.title: Gulf escalation: Riyadh airport strike kills 12, Iran claims a tanker mine strike, and Trump may join the fight
signals.what_happened: Saudi aviation authorities say a Saturday Oct 10 attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309; an American was among the victims. The Houthis claimed a Thursday strike on the same airport that killed three, and Washington blames them for Saturday's. Trump said Saturday the US 'may' join Saudi strikes on the Houthis and, asked whether his Oct 8 pledge not to strike Iran before the Nov 3 midterms still stands, said 'we're gonna take a look.' Iran's Revolutionary Guard said a crude supertanker hit a mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Oct 10 while using a route Iran has not approved; the ship was not named and the claim is not independently confirmed. On Oct 8 Treasury sanctioned 17 more vessels in Iran's shadow fleet.
signals.so_what: Who pays: oil importers and fuel heavy businesses, through a higher war premium. Who gets paid: producers with barrels outside the Gulf (XOM, CVX) and US refiners that run domestic crude. A mine claim matters more than one tanker, because insurers price the whole route; higher war risk cover means fewer ships try the strait. Second order: if the US joins Saudi strikes, the market will price more air and missile defense spending (RTX makes Patriot, which Saudi Arabia uses) and more Red Sea disruption. Third order: higher oil feeds Wednesday's CPI expectations and the Oct 28 Fed decision. Airlines (DAL, UAL) are the most exposed equities. What would make this wrong: a quick Saudi and Houthi de-escalation, Trump reaffirming the no strike pledge, or the tanker claim turning out to be false. Wait for Monday's oil open before acting; do not chase energy into a gap on light volume.

signals.title: Isaias: Gulf shut ins peaked near 72%, crews head back, still no refinery damage report
signals.since_yesterday: Shut ins rose to about 1.46 million barrels a day (about 72% of Gulf output) on Friday, and Chevron says it is sending crews back to its platforms through Sunday; there is still no damage report from Pascagoula or Saraland.
signals.what_happened: Federal data reported by Bloomberg and Oilprice put Friday's Gulf shut in at about 1.46 million barrels a day, roughly 72% of regional output, up from about 63% on Thursday. Chevron says four of its operated platforms kept producing, five were shut, and crew remobilization continues through Sunday. Regulators say undamaged platforms restart right after standard checks. In Alabama, outages topped 325,000 by 8am Saturday, about 24,800 of them in Mobile County, with downed trees and lines in Mobile. As of Sunday morning no source reports damage or a shutdown at Chevron's Pascagoula refinery or Vertex's Saraland refinery.
signals.so_what: The pattern so far is the good one: a big offshore shut in that comes back in days, and refineries outside the worst of the storm. Mobile County's outage count is modest, which lowers the odds of a long power loss at Saraland, but it is not a damage report. For XOM and CVX the storm reason to wait is fading; the Gulf attacks are now the bigger driver. What would make this wrong: a Monday report of flooding or a shutdown at Pascagoula, which supplies jet fuel to Southeast airports.

signals.title: Two FDA approvals Friday change practice: immunotherapy after surgery for dMMR colon cancer, and a monthly olanzapine shot
signals.what_happened: On Oct 9 the FDA approved Roche's Tecentriq with FOLFOX chemotherapy as adjuvant treatment for stage III colon cancer with deficient mismatch repair (dMMR), the first immunotherapy based adjuvant regimen for this group. In the NCI sponsored ATOMIC trial (712 patients) the combination cut the risk of recurrence or death by 50%, with 3 year disease free survival of 86% versus 76% on chemotherapy alone. The subcutaneous form (Tecentriq Hybreza) got the same approval. The same day Teva and Medincell won approval for Weltruza, the first once monthly subcutaneous olanzapine injection for schizophrenia; Teva says it needs no loading dose, no oral overlap and no post shot observation, and expects US launch in the coming weeks. FDA also approved Asahi Kasei's pritelivir (Hovilpri) for resistant herpes in immunocompromised adults.
signals.so_what: For a clinician: guidelines already call for mismatch repair testing of every colon cancer, so the change is in treatment after the test, not in who gets tested. It adds months of checkpoint inhibitor infusions after surgery for these patients, which is new revenue for Roche and more infusion chair time for oncology practices. Weltruza's selling point is removing the 3 hour observation and certified site rule that limits the older intramuscular olanzapine shot; if prescribers agree, it could take share from other long acting antipsychotic injections. Honest note: RHHBY has no dashboard verdict (not enough data) and TEVA is not on the dashboard, so these are watch items, not trades. What would make this wrong: payer pushback on cost, or real world injection site reactions.

signals.title: Medtronic's MiniMed swap closed Friday at the 4.5939 cap; results and share count change come next
signals.what_happened: Medtronic set the final exchange ratio for its MiniMed split-off at 4.5939 MiniMed shares per Medtronic share on Oct 7; the calculated ratio was higher, so the cap applied. The offer for up to 225.4 million MiniMed shares (about 80.1% of MiniMed, or the full 89.9% stake if oversubscribed) expired at the end of Oct 9. Medtronic will accept about 49 to 55 million of its own shares, with proration if too many are tendered. Final results were not out by Sunday.
signals.so_what: Who gets paid: Medtronic holders who stay, because the company retires shares without spending cash (MDT is Buy zone now on the dashboard at 88.48). Who pays: MiniMed, at least short term, because the shares just landed with Medtronic holders who did not choose to own a pump maker, and some will sell. Split-offs often see this kind of selling. Second order: a standalone MiniMed has to win on its own against Insulet and Tandem, which makes its Abbott sensor partnership more important. What would make this wrong: heavy proration showing weak demand, or MiniMed index buying absorbing the new float.

cycle.quadrant_why: September CPI is expected near 3.6% to 3.7% a year, up from 3.4%, and Brent is above $104 with Hormuz mostly shut since Feb 28. Growth is still positive and the S&P 500 sits near a record 7,811. In Dalio's four season view this is the rising inflation season.
cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Late. The Fed raised rates to 3.75% to 4.00% on Sep 16 and says another hike is possible, the 10-year yield is 5.24%, and stocks are near highs. Dalio's model: late in the short term debt cycle the central bank tightens to fight inflation, credit gets more expensive, and that tightening is what usually ends the expansion.
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. Government debt is high and long rates are above 5%, so each rate rise costs more to service. Dalio's model says this stage leaves policy makers little room: they cannot cut much without feeding inflation.
cycle.big_cycle: Of Dalio's five big forces, four are pushing at once: debt and money (high debt, high rates), internal order (a divided US heading into the Nov 3 midterms), external order (US China rivalry and a Gulf war), and technology (the AI spending boom, the one big tailwind).
tailwinds: The AI build out keeps spending flowing to chips, power and networking.
Oil and gas producers outside the Gulf earn more while Hormuz is disrupted.
Defense budgets rise in multiyear contracts.
headwinds: Rising inflation and rates hurt long duration growth stocks and anything with heavy debt.
An oil shock squeezes consumers, airlines and margins.
Late cycle tightening raises the odds of a slowdown in 2027.

history.what: Oil quadrupled and inflation surged. The S&P 500 fell about 48% from its January 1973 high to the October 1974 low, and even Exxon and Chevron fell about 44%.
history.lesson: In a true oil shock with rising inflation, almost nothing is safe. Cash and short duration held up best.

source.title: Museum of American Finance: 1970s Bear Market

history.what: Oil nearly doubled from Aug 2 to Oct 11, 1990, and the S&P 500 fell about 17% over the same window. When the air campaign began in January 1991, stocks rose almost 20% in about a month.
history.lesson: War scares hit fast, but markets bottom when the uncertainty peaks, often before the news gets better.

source.title: TrendSpider: The Gulf War recession 1990 to 1991

history.what: The S&P 500 lost about 19% for the year and entered a bear market in June, while the energy sector returned more than 60%, the best sector by far.
history.lesson: In the rising inflation season, energy and real assets lead and long duration growth lags.

source.title: Investing Daily: The Leaders and Laggards of 2022

cycle.differences: Today differs from 1973 in one big way: the AI spending boom is a real growth engine that did not exist then, and the US now produces much of its own oil. That is why the index is at a record despite $100 oil. The risk is that the AI trade is crowded, so a rate shock would hit it hard.
cycle.for_you: Swing: favor setups in the rising inflation winners (energy, defense, AI infrastructure with real earnings) and keep position sizes normal, not big; late cycle breakouts fail more often, so insist on breakout volume. Puts: sell only on names you would hold through a 20% drop, because history says oil shocks can bring one; do not reach for yield. Long term: buy quality in tranches, not all at once, and keep some cash for the kind of drawdown 1990 and 2022 delivered.

principle.text: Balance risk in ways that keep the big upside while reducing the downside.
principle.applied: Stay invested in the AI and energy trends that are working, but cap each position, use stops on swings, and keep cash ready. You do not need to predict the top to survive it.
